Full text

Abstract

The Japanese word 'kawaii' describes not only an object's cute attributes but also a positive feeling toward it. Although viewing cute objects can improve mood and encourage prosocial behavior, it remains unclear whether intentionally focusing on kawaii feelings enhances these effects. In two online experiments, participants viewed pictures of dogs and cats (N = 282) and other animals (N = 435). They were instructed to either find and savor the kawaii aspects of the animals or to find and describe their objective characteristics. The results showed that the picture ratings of valence, arousal, approach motivation, and kawaii were higher in the kawaii condition than in the objective condition. However, no significant differences were found between the conditions in terms of mood change or donation-related voluntary actions. Focusing on kawaii aspects can improve affective evaluation, but a one-time savoring session may not be sufficient to alter mood or behavior.

Psychology of cuteness and kawaii

People are frequently exposed to cute content in their daily lives, particularly on social media (Golonka et al., 2023). Research has shown that cute pictures are rated as more pleasant and elicit stronger smiling responses than neutral pictures (Nittono & Ihara, 2017). They are also associated with feelings of healing (Chou et al., 2022) or kama muta, a heartwarming feeling of being moved (Steinnes et al., 2019). Myrick (2015) surveyed 6,795 internet users and suggested that people may watch cat videos and look at cat pictures, which are often described as cute, as an easily accessible means of emotion regulation. However, it remains unclear whether these positive responses are automatically triggered by mere exposure or they can be intentionally enhanced by changing the way people view these stimuli.

The research on cuteness has started with the concept of Kindernschema (baby schema).

In his seminal monograph, Lorenz (1943) suggested that infantile features, such as a large head, rounded body, and chubby cheeks, elicit positive feelings and caregiving behavior. These features have been shown to increase perceived cuteness and caregiving motivation (Glocker et al., 2009) and activate reward-related brain regions (Kringelbach et al., 2008). Despite its intuitive appeal, the concept of baby schema has been inconsistently used, and its evolutionary significance remains unclear (Kawaguchi & Waller, 2024). Garsmeur and Baumard (2026) recently proposed that cuteness motivates developmental investment in inexperienced individuals beyond mere protection.

The present study focuses on the feelings evoked by cute objects rather than on their physical features. While the English word 'cuteness' mainly refers to an object's physical and perceptual attributes (Buckley, 2016), the Japanese concept of 'kawaii' includes both these attributes and the feelings evoked in the perceiver (Nittono, 2016; Nittono et al., 2023). In the latter sense, kawaii can be understood as a subjective emotional experience arising from cognitive appraisal and associated with approach motivation, such as wanting to get closer, keep watching, and care for the object (Nittono, 2016). Throughout this article, the term kawaii is used to include this emotional aspect.

Effects of evaluative dimensions and savoring

Recent studies have suggested that perceived cuteness is shaped not only by physical features but also by cognitive factors. Cuteness ratings can change through perceptual adaptation (Golle et al., 2013), familiarization (Hunt et al., 2023; Hunt & De Pascalis, 2024), and the objects' temperament (Parsons et al., 2014) and personality description (Takamatsu et al., 2023). For example, Takamatsu et al. (2023) found that pairing children's faces with positive personality descriptions increased perceived cuteness, whereas negative descriptions decreased it, and these changes in cuteness mediated the effects of the descriptions on nurturing motivation. Contextual information, knowledge, and experience can influence perceived cuteness, even when an object's physical features remain unchanged.

Psychological responses to cuteness-related stimuli can change depending on how they are evaluated. Nittono and Ohashi (2024) found that smiling-related facial muscle activity was stronger when participants rated the cuteness rather than the beauty of infant faces. Turner-Collins and Breitenbecher (2019) showed that evaluating dogs on humanlike rather than canine traits reduced subsequent pain intensity in the presence of a therapy dog. These examples suggest that changing the way people view a stimulus may alter its consequences.

One way to change the perspective is by savoring (Bryant, 1989), which involves intentionally attending to and appreciating positive experiences to enhance and maintain positive emotions (Bryant, 2021; Bryant et al., 2011). Experimental studies have shown that savoring can enhance evaluations of positive stimuli and emotional well-being (see Chen et al., 2026, for a recent review). Wilson and MacNamara (2021) found that focusing on the positive aspects of pictures increased their pleasantness ratings, with the effect persisting when the pictures were later viewed without savoring instructions. This effect also generalized to novel pictures from previously savored categories, although generalization was observed for animal but not people pictures (Wilson & MacNamara, 2024). Other studies have found that savoring alleviates negative emotions and improves positive emotions after experiencing stress or worry (Klibert et al., 2022; Rosen & LaFreniere, 2023).

Prosocial behavior and kawaii

Previous research suggests that cute stimuli promote prosocial intentions, including conservation and donation intentions (Baek et al., 2025; Phan et al., 2026; Shin & Mattila, 2021; T. Wang et al., 2017). Beyond subjective reports of intention, Takamatsu and Nittono (in press) demonstrated that young animals were rated as cuter than adult animals and received more mouse clicks in a click-donation task in which the number of voluntary mouse clicks during a fixed period determined the amount of money to donate. Such prosocial effects of cute stimuli may reflect broader human sociality rather than caregiving alone (Sherman & Haidt, 2011).

Cute stimuli may promote prosocial behavior through the positive feeling of kawaii, since positive affect facilitates prosociality (Lyubomirsky et al., 2005). If finding and savoring kawaii aspects of animals increases positive affect, it may promote prosocial behavior toward animals.

Purposes of the present study

This study examined whether finding and savoring kawaii aspects of animal pictures improves affective ratings of the pictures, momentary mood, and prosocial behavior toward animals, compared with finding and describing their objective characteristics.

Participants were instructed to try to look for the kawaii aspects of animal pictures and to savor the positive feelings that arose from doing so. Animals were selected because they are typical cute stimuli (Borgi et al., 2014) and have been used in previous research on savoring (Wilson & MacNamara, 2024). The click-donation task (Takamatsu & Nittono, in press) was used to test the effect on prosocial behavior.

There were three hypotheses: Participants in the kawaii condition would report more positive picture ratings (H1), greater increases in positive mood and decreases in negative mood (H2), and greater prosocial behavior toward animals (H3) than those in the objective condition. The experiments were preregistered: Experiments 1 (https://osf.io/b7wpz/) and 2 (https://osf.io/e4qt8/). The stimulus material and raw data are available at https://osf.io/fu27c/.

Experiment 1

Method

Design and power analysis

Experiment 1 used a between-participants design with a factor of the viewing condition (kawaii or objective). For mood outcomes, time (pre-or post-task) was included as a within-participants factor. Chen et al. (2026) reported an overall medium effect of savoring interventions (Hedges' g = 0.51). In this study, a more conservative small effect (f = .10) was assumed for the power analysis. G*Power Version 3.1.9.6 (Faul et al., 2009) indicated that 200 participants were required for 80% power to detect the condition × time interaction at α = .05, assuming a repeated-measures correlation of .50.

Participants

A total of 300 participants were recruited through a crowdsourcing service (Lancers, Tokyo, Japan) to compensate for potential data loss. Participants were adults aged 18 years or older who had experienced feelings of kawaii toward dogs or cats, had normal

Stimuli

Four animal pictures (two dogs: 1044.jpg, 1079.jpg; two cats: 2009.jpg, 2100.jpg) were selected from the Animal Affective Picture System (AAPS; Nittono & Nakamura, 2026), which provides normative 9-point ratings (1-9) of valence, arousal, motivational direction (approach-avoidance), and kawaii (cuteness). To avoid ceiling and floor effects, pictures were selected with ratings close to the median values of the 225 dog and cat pictures in the AAPS. The mean ratings of the selected pictures were 6.38, 4.88, 6.42, and 6.59, for valence, arousal, motivational direction, and kawaii, respectively. All animals faced forward, and both eyes were visible.

Dependent variables

Picture rating. Each picture was rated for valence, arousal, motivational direction, kawaii, and willingness to care for the animal (hereinafter, willingness to care) on 9point scales (valence:1 = very negative,5 = neutral,9 = very positive; arousal:1 = calm,5 = neutral,9 = excited; motivational direction:1 = to avoid,5 = neutral,9 = to approach; kawaii:1 = not at all kawaii,9 = extremely kawaii; willingness to care:1 = not at all,9 = very much). Mood questionnaire. Mood was assessed using the Temporary Mood Scale (Tokuda, 2011), which consists of six three-item subscales (tension, depression, anger, confusion, fatigue, and vigor) rated on a 5-point scale (1 = not at all applicable,5 = very applicable). In the present study, Cronbach's α calculated separately for pre-and posttask ratings ranged from .86 to .88 for vigor and from .70 to .92 for the five negative mood subscales, comparable to previously reported values (α = .78-.87; Tokuda, 2007).

The sum of the three vigor items was used as the positive mood index, and the mean of the summed scores of the other five subscales was used as the negative mood index (ranges: 3-15).

Procedure

Figure 1 illustrates the experimental procedure. First, the participants completed the mood questionnaire and then performed the picture-viewing task. In the kawaii condition, participants were instructed to find the kawaii aspects of each animal and experience the resulting feeling of kawaii, whereas those in the objective condition were instructed to identify its objective characteristics. Both groups then described the identified aspects in writing. The full instructions are provided in Table S1.

Each trial began with a preview of an animal picture for 3 s, followed by viewing instructions and presentation of the same picture for 12 s. Participants then described its kawaii aspects or objective characteristics and rated the picture for valence, arousal, motivational direction, kawaii, and willingness to care. The four pictures were presented in random order. After completing the viewing task, the participants completed the mood questionnaire again.

After reading a text about the situation of sheltered dogs and cats in Japan (see Table S1 for the full text), the participants were offered an optional donation task in which each mouse click within 5 s resulted in a 1-yen donation by the researcher to an animal welfare organization. They then reported how they had viewed the pictures to check their understanding of the task. Finally, they rated how kawaii they usually found dogs and cats separately (1 = not at all kawaii,5 = very kawaii) and reported whether they had ever owned a dog or a cat.

Statistical analysis

H1 was tested using linear mixed models for each picture rating, with viewing condition (kawaii or objective) as a fixed effect and participants and pictures as random effects: rating ~ viewing condition + (1 | participant) + (1 | picture). Fixed effects were tested using Type III sums of squares with Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom. H2 was tested using a 2 (viewing condition: kawaii or objective) × 2 (time: pre-or post-task) mixed ANOVA on the positive and negative mood scores. H3 was tested by comparing donation-task participation rates using a chi-square test and, among those who participated, the number of clicks using Welch's t-test. Following Takamatsu and Nittono (in press), click counts were log10-transformed after adding 1, and the analysis was repeated using raw scores.

Analyses were conducted using JASP version 0.98.1 (JASP Team, 2026), except that LMM effect sizes were calculated using R Statistical Software version 4.6.1 (R Core Team, 2026) with the effectsize package version 1.0.3 (Ben-Shachar et al., 2020). The significance level was α = .05.

Manipulation check and exploratory analysis

As a manipulation check, free descriptions were analyzed using KH Coder (Version 3. Beta.04; Higuchi, 2016), and the occurrences of the word 'kawaii' and their proportion among all extracted words were calculated after morphological analysis. The frequency and proportion were expected to be higher in the kawaii condition than in the objective condition.

As an exploratory analysis, ANCOVAs were used to examine condition differences in positive and negative mood changes (post -pre), controlling for pre-task mood. The effects of individual difference variables, such as general kawaii feelings toward animals and ownership experience, were analyzed. Because these analyses are not directly related to the research question, their full results are reported in the Supplementary Material.

Results

Manipulation check

Based on the preregistered exclusion criteria, 18 participants were excluded for failing the instruction-comprehension check (n = 9) or the comprehension checks for the donation task (n = 9). The final sample consisted of 282 participants (90 women, 192 men; age range: 24-79 years, M = 45.1, SD = 9.6). Participant characteristics by condition are shown in Table 1, with no significant differences between conditions.

Free-description time was shorter in the kawaii condition than in the objective condition (p = .003), whereas the number of characters did not differ significantly (see Table S2 for details). 'Kawaii' was the most frequent word that appeared in the kawaii condition (509 occurrences, 9.6%) but ranked 49th in the objective condition (24 occurrences, 0.4%; see Table S3 for details).

The total number of mouse clicks in the donation task was 4,048, including those of participants not included in the analysis. As explained to the participants, 5,000 yen was donated to a public-interest incorporated association for animal welfare (Animal Donation, Japan).

Picture ratings

Table 2 shows the estimated marginal means of the picture ratings. The corresponding raincloud plots are shown in Figure S1. The viewing condition had a significant effect on all five ratings. Participants in the kawaii condition rated the pictures higher than those in the objective condition on valence, arousal, motivational direction, kawaii, and willingness to care (ps < .016).

Mood changes

Table 3 shows the mean mood scores before and after the task, and Table 4 shows the results of the mixed ANOVAs. The corresponding raincloud plots are shown in Figures S2 and S3. The main effect of time was significant for both positive and negative mood, with positive mood increasing and negative mood decreasing from pre-to post-task.

Neither the main effect of viewing condition nor the condition × time interaction was significant (ps > .075), although the increase in positive mood (range: -12 to +12) was descriptively larger in the kawaii condition (M = 1.00) than in the objective condition (M = 0.59).

Exploratory ANCOVAs showed that higher pre-task positive mood was associated with smaller increases in positive mood, F(1, 279) = 24.15, p < .001, ηp² = .08. After controlling for pre-task positive mood, the effect of viewing condition was significant, F(1, 279) = 4.56, p = .034, ηp² = .02. Higher pre-task negative mood was associated with larger decreases in negative mood, F(1, 279) = 74.34, p < .001, ηp² = .21.

However, the effect of viewing condition after controlling for pre-task negative mood was not significant, F(1, 279) = 0.79, p = .374, ηp² = .00.

Prosocial behavior

Donation-task participation did not differ between the kawaii (119/140, 85.0%) and objective conditions (118/142, 83.1%), χ 2 (1) = 0.19, p = .663. Among participants who took part in the task (n = 237), log10-transformed click counts also did not differ between conditions (kawaii: M = 1.16, SD = 0.37; objective: M = 1.11, SD = 0.38), t(234.87) = 1.11, p = .269, d = 0.14. The same conclusion was obtained for raw click counts (kawaii: M = 17.70, SD = 10.12; objective: M = 15.78, SD = 9.67), t(234.68) = 1.49, p = .137, d = 0.19.

Discussion

Experiment 1 showed that finding and savoring kawaii aspects of animal pictures increased all five picture ratings. These findings suggest that focusing on different aspects of an object can modify subjective evaluations. However, finding and savoring kawaii aspects did not improve post-task mood or prosocial behavior. Experiment 1 had several limitations. First, participants in the kawaii condition spent less time on free description than those in the objective condition, so differences in task duration may have influenced the results. Second, dogs and cats are typical companion animals (Pongrácz & Dobos, 2023), and it remained unclear whether the effects would generalize to less familiar species. Third, the mood questionnaire had a significant disparity in the number of positive and negative items: three for positive mood and 15 for negative mood. Fourth, the sample included about twice as many men as women. To address these issues, the following changes were made in Experiment 2: (1) a standard description time of 90 s was set; (2) different animals than dogs and cats were used; (3) mood was assessed with the Japanese version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; Watson et al., 1988; Sato & Yasuda, 2001); and (4) approximately equal numbers of men and women were recruited.

Experiment 2

Method

Participants

The same power analysis as in Experiment 1 was used, with recruitment increased to 250 women and 250 men to enable exploratory analyses by gender. Recruitment and procedures were otherwise the same as in Experiment 1, except that eligibility and exclusion criteria concerning kawaii feelings referred to animals in general rather than specifically to dogs or cats. Data were collected on July 5 and 6, 2026. Experiment 2 was approved by the same committee (HB-R8-034).

Stimuli and dependent variables

Four pictures of animals other than dogs and cats (mouse: 3242.jpg; donkey: 4235.jpg; owl: 7225.jpg; otter: 6203.jpg) were selected from the AAPS to approximate the kawaii ratings of the Experiment 1 stimuli while minimizing differences in valence, arousal, and motivational direction. Their mean normative ratings were 6.30, 4.89, 6.14, and 6.59 for valence, arousal, motivational direction, and kawaii, respectively. As in Experiment 1, all animals faced forward, with both eyes visible.

Mood was assessed using the 16-item Japanese version of the PANAS (Sato & Yasuda, 2001) rather than the original 20-item version (Watson et al., 1988). The eight positive and eight negative items were rated on a 6-point scale (1 = not at all,6 = extremely) and summed separately. Cronbach's α calculated separately for pre-and post-task ratings was .89-.90 for positive affect and .93-.94 for negative affect, comparable to previously reported values for current affect (.90 and .91, respectively; Sato & Yasuda, 2001).

The instructions, picture rating scales, and prosocial behavior measures were the same as in Experiment 1, except that 'dogs and cats' were replaced with 'animals.' As individual-difference measures, participants rated how kawaii they usually found animals (1 = not at all kawaii,5 = very kawaii), their impression of experiencing the feeling of kawaii (1 = negative,5 = positive), how frequently they used the word 'kawaii' (1 = not at all,5 = very frequently), and the perceived difficulty of free description (1 = easy,5 = difficult), and reported whether they had ever owned animals.

Procedure

The procedure was the same as in Experiment 1, except that a standard duration for description (90 s) was set for each picture. After 90 s, the Next Page button appeared, allowing participants to proceed.

Statistical analysis

The analyses were the same as in Experiment 1.

Results

Manipulation check

Participants were excluded for failing the instruction-comprehension check (n = 41) or donation-task comprehension checks (n = 24), or for reporting that they never found animals kawaii (n = 1); one participant met both of the first two criteria. No participant provided invalid free descriptions. The final sample consisted of 435 participants (217 women and 218 men; age range: 21-72 years, M = 45.9, SD = 10.3). Table 1 shows that the two conditions did not differ significantly in demographic or individual difference variables, except that free description was rated as less difficult in the kawaii condition.

Neither free-description time nor character counts differed significantly between conditions (ps > .143, see Table S2 for details). 'Kawaii' was the most frequent word that appeared in the kawaii condition (974 occurrences, 9.1%) but ranked 23rd in the objective condition (85 occurrences, 0.7%; see Table S4 for details).

The total number of mouse clicks in the donation task was 5,792, including those of participants not included in the analysis. As explained to the participants, 6,000 yen was donated to the same association for animal welfare as in Experiment 1.

Picture ratings

Table 2 shows the estimated marginal means of the picture ratings. The corresponding raincloud plots are shown in Figure S1. Participants in the kawaii condition rated the pictures significantly higher than those in the objective condition on valence, arousal, motivational direction, and kawaii (ps < .006), with a similar tendency for willingness to care (p = .054).

Mood changes

Table 3 shows the mean mood scores, and Table 4 shows the ANOVA results. The corresponding raincloud plots are shown in Figures S2 and S3. The main effect of time was significant for both positive and negative affect, with positive affect increasing and negative affect decreasing from pre-to post-task. Neither the main effect of viewing condition nor the condition × time interaction was significant (ps > .069), although the increase in positive affect (range: -40 to +40) was descriptively larger in the kawaii condition (M = 1.15) than in the objective condition (M = 0.28).

Exploratory ANCOVAs showed significant effects of pre-task mood on both positive affect change, F(1, 432) = 19.22, p < .001, ηp² = .04, and negative affect change, F(1, 432) = 182.10, p < .001, ηp² = .30. After controlling for pre-task mood, viewing condition did not significantly affect either positive or negative affect change (ps > .105).

Prosocial behavior

Donation-task participation did not differ between the kawaii (175/222, 78.8%) and objective conditions (169/213, 79.3%), χ 2 (1) = 0.02, p = .895. Among the participants who took part in the task (n = 344), log10-transformed click counts also did not differ between conditions (kawaii: M = 1.02, SD = 0.42; objective: M = 1.07, SD = 0.35), t(334.69) = 1.18, p = .239, d = 0.13. The same conclusion was obtained for raw click counts (kawaii: M = 13.87, SD = 10.08; objective: M = 14.19, SD = 9.12), t(340.60) = 0.31, p = .757, d = 0.03.

Discussion

Experiment 2 was conducted to replicate the findings of Experiment 1 by addressing several technical concerns. Similar to Experiment 1, finding and savoring the kawaii aspects of animal pictures increased ratings of valence, arousal, motivational direction, and kawaii ratings, with a similar tendency for willingness to care. This suggests that the effect was not limited to dogs and cats. The weaker effect on willingness to care may be because the animals used in Experiment 2 were less likely to be perceived as care targets than dogs and cats (Possidónio et al., 2019).

Effects on mood and prosocial behavior were not observed again. The effect on positive mood change found in Experiment 1 after controlling for pre-task mood was not replicated. No condition differences were found in donation-task participation or the number of clicks.

General discussion

Across the two experiments, finding and savoring the kawaii aspects of animal pictures increased picture ratings, supporting H1, whereas no clear effects were found on mood (H2) or prosocial behavior (H3).

Change in picture ratings

Finding kawaii aspects of animal pictures and savoring the evoked feelings enhanced evaluations of the pictures in both experiments, consistent with findings that focusing on positive aspects of pictures increases their ratings (Wilson & MacNamara, 2021 , 2024). Because 'kawaii' and 'cute' have positive connotations (Nittono, 2016; Nittono et al., 2021), the instruction to find kawaii aspects is virtually the same as focusing on the positive aspects of the pictures.

Higher kawaii ratings in the kawaii condition may partly reflect demand characteristics.

However, valence and approach motivation ratings also increased, despite not being mentioned in the instructions. This pattern agrees with kawaii as a positive emotion associated with approach motivation (Nittono, 2016), suggesting that finding kawaii aspects influences broader affective and motivational evaluations. While previous research has primarily examined physical features that make stimuli cute (e.g., Aradhye et al., 2015; Borgi et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2022), the present findings show that viewing the same stimulus from different perspectives can also shape responses to it.

Task difficulty provides an alternative explanation. Easier processing can produce more positive evaluations (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009), and the objective task appeared more difficult; participants spent more time on free description in Experiment 1 and rated the task as more difficult in Experiment 2. Task difficulty may have contributed to the condition differences in picture ratings.

Change in mood

Positive mood increased and negative mood decreased after viewing animal pictures, but the effect of kawaii and objective conditions on mood change was not significant.

The mood improvement may be partly due to viewing cute animal pictures (Myrick, 2015). However, simply viewing animal pictures does not necessarily improve mood (Machová & Flegr, 2025). Although there was no passive-viewing condition in this study, the improvement may result from the active processing of the pictures required in both conditions.

Although the increase in positive mood was descriptively larger in the kawaii condition in both experiments, the lack of significant interactions suggests that the effect of finding and savoring kawaii on mood was small. The objective condition also required close attention to potentially positive (cute) stimuli and may thus have shared some features of savoring. In a meta-analysis paper, Chen et al. (2026) mentioned that the effect of savoring interventions is smaller when compared to active control conditions than passive control conditions. Unlike previous studies using neutral stimuli or different control tasks (e.g., Klibert et al., 2022; Rosen & LaFreniere, 2023), the present conditions differed mainly in the perspective from which the pictures were viewed.

These task features may have limited the observed effect of savoring kawaii on mood.

Prosocial behavior

Previous studies have shown that cuteness promotes donation intentions (Baek et al., 2025; Phan et al., 2026) and donation-related behavior (Takamatsu & Nittono, in press).

In the present study, however, no significant differences in donation behavior were found between conditions. In their scoping review, Thomas-Walters et al. ( 2020)suggested that showing animal images can promote viewers' protective attitudes toward the animals, particularly when they find the animals aesthetically pleasing. However, this does not always result in actual behavior. Considering that positive mood can promote prosocial behavior (Lyubomirsky et al., 2005), the lack of a mood difference between conditions may partly explain the absence of an effect on donations. In addition, whereas participants in Takamatsu and Nittono (in press) donated to help the pictured animals, the present donation task concerned sheltered animals in general.

Given the increased willingness to care for the animals, the effects of finding kawaii aspects may have been specific to the animals actually viewed rather than other animals in general. Perceiving and savoring kawaii may produce short-term effects on responses toward concrete targets rather than influencing general prosociality.

Limitations and future directions

This study has several limitations. First, the Japanese sample limits cultural generalizability. Because Japanese kawaii encompasses both object characteristics and perceivers' positive feelings and is used more broadly than comparable English and Spanish terms (Nittono et al., 2023), future studies should examine whether savoring kawaii is also effective in different cultures.

Second, only animal pictures were used. Because savoring effects were generalized to novel animal pictures but not people pictures (Wilson & MacNamara, 2024), and kawaii pictures with and without baby schema elicited partly different responses (Nittono & Ihara, 2017), future studies should examine whether similar effects occur for other kawaii stimuli, such as infants and objects.

Third, it is unclear whether the participants actually savored the evoked feelings. The instructions encouraged participants to experience kawaii but not explicitly to attend to and maintain the feelings, which are central to savoring (Bryant, 2021; Bryant & Veroff, 2007). Previous brief interventions have involved attending to positive stimuli or memories and their evoked feelings for 10-15 min, which was longer than in this study (Klibert et al., 2022; B. A. Wang et al., 2023). Furthermore, verbalizing positive experiences may be less beneficial than imagining or replaying them (Holmes et al., 2006; Lyubomirsky et al., 2006). Future studies should use more explicit savoring instructions and assess the extent of savoring and the duration of positive feelings (e.g., Rosen & LaFreniere, 2023).

Fourth, no passive control condition was included. Such a condition would help determine whether the mood improvement observed in both conditions resulted from merely viewing the pictures or from actively processing them.

Conclusion

The two experiments consistently showed that the instruction to find and savor kawaii aspects of animal pictures enhanced participants' evaluations of these pictures, but it did not reliably influence mood or prosocial behavior. Since people like cute things and the feeling of kawaii depends not only on stimulus characteristics but also on how people view the stimulus, this "savoring kawaii" approach is easily applicable to everyday situations and is a potentially useful way of emotional regulation.

Analyses of Individual Difference Variables

Responses to animal pictures may depend on viewers' characteristics. People who usually find animals kawaii may rate animal pictures more positively and be more willing to care for animals. Pet ownership is associated with positive attitudes toward animals (Auger & Amiot, 2017) and more positive ratings of animal pictures (Possidónio et al., 2019). The present analyses examined whether general kawaii feelings, previous ownership, and gender were related to the outcomes and moderated the effects of the viewing instructions. Previous ownership was expected to be associated with higher general kawaii feelings, and both were expected to be positively associated with picture ratings, mood improvement, and prosocial behavior. Gender was examined exploratorily.

Method

The association between previous ownership and general kawaii feelings toward animals was first examined. General kawaii feelings were indexed by the mean of the ratings for dogs and cats in Experiment 1 and by a single rating for animals in general in Experiment 2. ANCOVAs were then conducted on the picture ratings, mood change scores, and the number of clicks, with viewing condition, general kawaii feelings, previous ownership, gender, and the interactions of viewing condition with each of these variables. Continuous variables were mean-centered, and binary variables were coded using weighted effect coding to account for unequal group sizes (te Grotenhuis et al., 2017). Participation in the donation task was analyzed using logistic regression with the same predictors.

Results

Participants with previous pet ownership reported higher general kawaii feelings toward animals than those without (Experiment 1: r = .24; Experiment 2: r = .27; ps < .001). After controlling for the individual difference variables, the effects of viewing condition on all five picture ratings were significant in both experiments (Table S5), including willingness to care in Experiment 2, which was not significant in the preregistered analysis. The effects of viewing condition on mood change, the number of clicks, and donation-task participation remained nonsignificant (Tables S6-S8).

Participants with higher general kawaii feelings gave higher picture ratings, showed greater increases in positive mood, made more clicks, and were more likely to participate in the donation task in both experiments. They also showed a greater decrease in negative mood in Experiment 1 only. Previous ownership was related only to fewer clicks in Experiment 1. In Experiment 1, women gave higher valence, arousal, and kawaii ratings and showed a greater decrease in negative mood than men; gender was not related to any outcome in Experiment 2. Interactions between viewing condition and the individual difference variables were mostly nonsignificant, and none of the significant interactions was replicated across the two experiments.

Discussion

General kawaii feelings toward animals were related to most of the outcome variables, and controlling for these individual differences did not change the effects of viewing condition on picture ratings. As expected, previous ownership was associated with higher general kawaii feelings but was largely unrelated to the outcomes. The higher picture ratings by pet owners in previous research (Possidónio et al., 2019) may therefore partly reflect their general kawaii feelings.

Conclusion

Across both experiments, general kawaii feelings toward animals, rather than previous ownership or gender, were consistently related to responses to the animal pictures and donation behavior. The effects of the viewing instructions on picture ratings did not depend on these individual differences.
